symbol_descriptions: Time rate of change of the sphere's downward velocity
Downward velocity of the sphere through the viscous oil
Effective gravitational acceleration accounting for buoyancy (net downward pull per unit mass)
derivation_notes: Newton's second law for a sphere in viscous oil: net gravity minus buoyancy drives descent, while linear (Stokes) drag opposes motion, yielding an approach to terminal velocity.

states.description: Downward velocity of the sphere through the viscous oil

scenario_text: A small solid sphere is released from rest into a tall column of viscous oil. As it falls, the drag force grows with speed until it balances the net gravitational pull, and the sphere approaches a steady descent velocity. We track how the vertical velocity evolves over time from the moment of release.

symbol_descriptions: Steady volumetric flow rate through the pipe
Pressure difference across the pipe length
derivation_notes: Hagen-Poiseuille law for laminar steady flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid in a long straight cylindrical pipe, derived from the Navier-Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions.
scenario_text: Steady flow of a fluid through a long straight pipe is driven by a pressure difference across its ends. For a given fluid and pipe geometry, the volumetric throughput responds to the applied pressure gradient and depends strongly on the internal radius. We measure the instantaneous flow rate as conditions are varied.

symbol_descriptions: Phase speed of a small-amplitude surface gravity wave
derivation_notes: Derived from the linear dispersion relation for surface gravity waves, omega^2 = g*k*tanh(k*h) with k=2*pi/lam and c=omega/k, valid for arbitrary depth and reproducing both deep-water and shallow-water limits.
scenario_text: A shallow water surface is disturbed and small-amplitude gravity waves propagate across it. The speed at which each wave crest travels depends on the wavelength and on the local depth of the fluid layer. We record the propagation speed under different combinations of wavelength and depth.

symbol_descriptions: Growth rate of the interface perturbation amplitude in the shear layer.
Amplitude of the interfacial ripple between the two streams.
Linear Kelvin-Helmholtz growth rate set by the velocity difference and shear layer scale.
Saturation amplitude at which nonlinear roll-up limits further growth.
derivation_notes: The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability gives exponential growth of a small interface ripple at rate sigma_max drawn from the shear; nonlinear saturation as the perturbation reaches the shear-layer thickness limits the amplitude, yielding a logistic growth law.

states.description: Amplitude of the interfacial ripple between the two streams.

scenario_text: Two adjacent parallel streams of fluid move at different speeds, creating a thin shear layer between them. A small sinusoidal ripple at the interface can grow when the velocity difference is large enough, drawing energy from the shear. We follow the amplitude of the interface perturbation as it develops in time.

symbol_descriptions: Local Mach ratio of flow speed to local sound speed in the subsonic branch
Ratio of local cross-sectional area to throat area
Ratio of specific heats of the gas
derivation_notes: This is the area-Mach number relation for isentropic quasi-one-dimensional compressible flow, derived from conservation of mass with isentropic density-Mach relations; the subsonic branch (M<1) is selected.
scenario_text: A gas flows steadily through a smoothly narrowing then widening duct that includes a throat. The local flow speed relative to the local sound speed varies along the duct, and this ratio governs whether the flow accelerates or decelerates as the cross-section changes. For fixed reservoir conditions we evaluate the local Mach ratio as a function of area ratio in the subsonic branch.

symbol_descriptions: Time rate of change of the peak dye concentration at the injection center
Peak dye concentration at the center of the spreading patch
dimensionality-dependent decay exponent factor for diffusive spreading
derivation_notes: For a diffusing point-source patch, the peak concentration follows a power law C ~ t^(-n) (n = dimension/2 for Fickian diffusion), giving the self-similar decay dC/dt = -n*C/t.

states.description: Peak dye concentration at the center of the spreading patch

scenario_text: A localized patch of dye is injected into a fluid at rest and spreads outward purely by molecular diffusion. The peak concentration at the injection point decreases over time as the dye disperses through the surrounding medium. We monitor how the centerline concentration relaxes as the patch broadens.

symbol_descriptions: Time rate of change of the volume-averaged turbulent kinetic energy
Volume-averaged turbulent kinetic energy of the fluid
derivation_notes: After forcing stops, turbulent kinetic energy decays through dissipation whose rate scales as k^(3/2)/L, following the standard eddy-turnover closure epsilon ~ k^(3/2)/L.

states.description: Volume-averaged turbulent kinetic energy of the fluid

scenario_text: Turbulent kinetic energy is generated in a stirred region of fluid and then decays once the forcing is removed. The energy is dissipated at a rate that depends on the current energy level and a characteristic eddy length scale. We track the volume-averaged turbulent energy as it declines after stirring stops.

symbol_descriptions: Time rate of change of the local liquid film thickness
Local thickness of the draining liquid film
Characteristic vertical length scale over which flux varies
derivation_notes: The gravity-driven drainage flux per unit width is q = rho*g*h^3/(3*mu); local mass conservation gives dh/dt = -dq/dx, which for a self-similar thinning film scales as -(rho*g/mu)*h^2*(h/L_drain), so thicker films drain faster and the film thins monotonically.

states.description: Local thickness of the draining liquid film

scenario_text: A thin liquid film coats a vertical plate and drains downward under gravity, resisted by internal viscosity. The film thickness at a fixed height decreases as fluid flows away faster than it is replenished. We follow the local film thickness as it thins over time.

symbol_descriptions: Instantaneous drag force on the towed sphere
Towing speed of the sphere through the fluid
Reynolds-number correction coefficient bridging Stokes and inertial regimes
derivation_notes: Combines Stokes viscous drag (3*pi*mu*U*d) with a quadratic inertial drag (Newtonian regime, ~rho*U^2*d^2) and a Reynolds-number-dependent correction term proportional to sqrt(Re), capturing the transition from viscous- to inertia-dominated drag on a sphere.
scenario_text: A neutrally buoyant sphere is towed at constant speed through an unbounded fluid, and the resistive force it experiences depends on the flow speed and fluid properties. Across a wide range of towing speeds the character of the drag changes as inertial effects grow relative to viscous ones. We measure the instantaneous drag force under different towing speeds and fluid densities.

symbol_descriptions: Time rate of change of the bulk fluid angular velocity
Angular velocity of the bulk rotating fluid
derivation_notes: Spin-down of a rotating fluid is governed by Ekman pumping, which drives an exponential decay of the bulk angular velocity on the Ekman timescale, giving dw/dt = -w/tau_E.

states.description: Angular velocity of the bulk rotating fluid

scenario_text: Fluid within a long rotating cylindrical container is initially spinning with the walls, then the walls are suddenly stopped. Viscous coupling with the stationary boundary gradually brings the interior fluid rotation to rest. We follow the angular velocity of the bulk fluid as it spins down.

derivation_notes: Standard quantum-mechanical transmission coefficient for a rectangular barrier with E<V, obtained by matching wavefunctions across the classically forbidden region where the wavefunction decays as exp(-kappa*x) with kappa=sqrt(2*m*(V-E))/hbar.
scenario_text: A particle of fixed energy approaches a rectangular potential barrier whose height exceeds the particle energy. The probability of the particle emerging on the far side is measured as a function of barrier thickness. The experimenter varies the barrier width and records the transmission fraction. This probes how evanescent penetration governs quantum leakage through a classically forbidden region.

symbol_descriptions: energy of a bound stationary state
derivation_notes: Solving the time-independent Schrodinger equation for an infinite square well with impenetrable walls yields quantized standing-wave states with energies E_n = n^2 pi^2 hbar^2 / (2 m L^2).
scenario_text: A particle is confined to a one-dimensional box with impenetrable walls. The discrete energies of the allowed stationary states are recorded as a function of the quantum level index and the box length. The experimenter tunes the box size and identifies the level index of interest. This measures how confinement quantizes the allowed energies.

symbol_descriptions: energy spacing between adjacent vibrational levels
derivation_notes: The quantum harmonic oscillator has equally spaced levels E_n = hbar*omega*(n+1/2) with omega = sqrt(k/m); adjacent level spacing is dE = hbar*omega = hbar*sqrt(k/m).
scenario_text: Cold atoms are prepared in a harmonic trap and the spacing between adjacent vibrational levels is studied. The characteristic level separation is measured as the trap stiffness and particle mass are varied. This probes the equally spaced spectrum characteristic of a quadratic confining potential.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of excited-state population
derivation_notes: On resonance the optical Bloch equations reduce to a coupled pair: the population change is driven by the coherence, and the coherence responds to the population inversion (1 - 2P), yielding undamped Rabi oscillations of frequency Omega.

states.description: excited-state population
coherence between the two levels

scenario_text: A two-level quantum system is driven between its ground and excited configurations by a resonant coupling. The population of the excited state is followed over time as it cycles between the two levels. The measurement tracks coherent population transfer driven by the coupling strength. This captures the reversible exchange of probability amplitude in a coupled pair of states.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of wave packet spatial width
spatial width of the wave packet
derivation_notes: For a free Gaussian packet the variance obeys d(w^2)/dt = 2s and ds/dt = (hbar/m)^2, so w and its width-momentum correlation s form a closed pair reproducing the exact quadratic-in-time dispersive spreading.

states.description: spatial width of the wave packet
width-momentum correlation quantity coupling width growth to momentum spread

scenario_text: A localized wave packet is prepared in free space with an initial spatial spread and momentum uncertainty. As it propagates without any potential, its spatial width grows over time. The experiment follows the broadening of the packet width and its momentum spread. This probes dispersive spreading arising from the range of constituent wavelengths.

derivation_notes: From low-energy s-wave scattering theory using the effective range expansion k*cot(delta0) = -1/a + (1/2)*r*k^2, with sigma = 4*pi/k^2 * sin^2(delta0) = 4*pi/(1/a - r*k^2/2)^2 + k^2), where k^2 = 2*mass*E/hbar^2.
scenario_text: Particles scatter off a weak localized potential at low energy, and the total scattering cross section is measured. The experimenter varies the incoming particle energy and the strength of the potential. At low energies the response is dominated by a single isotropic channel. This probes how weak short-range scattering saturates with vanishing energy.

symbol_descriptions: binding energy of the shallow bound state
derivation_notes: This is the even-parity bound-state matching condition for a 1D finite square well: matching the logarithmic derivative of the interior cosine solution (wavenumber k=sqrt(2m(V-Eb))/hbar) to the exterior decaying exponential (decay kappa=sqrt(2m*Eb)/hbar) gives k*tan(k*L/2)=kappa, rewritten here with Eb the binding energy below threshold; near threshold this yields the characteristic nonlinear onset.
scenario_text: A single bound state supported by a shallow attractive finite-depth well is studied. The binding energy of the lone bound level is recorded as the well depth and width are varied. Near the threshold where the state just barely binds, the response shows a distinctive nonlinear onset. This probes the emergence of a bound level from an attractive potential.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of occupation probability in the right well
occupation probability of the right well
energy detuning between the two wells
derivation_notes: Two-level tunneling dynamics: the population transfer rate is set by the tunneling coupling times the coherence, while the coherence evolves under the population imbalance and detuning, producing coherent Rabi-like oscillations of the right-well occupation.

states.description: occupation probability of the right well
interwell coherence amplitude

scenario_text: A quantum particle is placed in a double-well configuration where it can tunnel between two nearly degenerate localized states. The probability of finding the particle in the initially unoccupied well oscillates coherently in time. The measurement follows the slow back-and-forth transfer set by the tunneling coupling. This captures coherent tunneling oscillation between two wells.

symbol_descriptions: energy shift of the bound level under the applied field
derivation_notes: Stationary perturbation theory (Stark effect) expansion of the bound-state energy in even powers of field: the leading term is the quadratic polarizability response and the next term is the quartic hyperpolarizability correction.
scenario_text: An electron in a bound level is subjected to a static uniform field that deforms its confining potential. The shift of the level energy is measured as the applied field strength is increased from zero. For moderate fields the energy correction grows as a smooth polynomial response. This probes the field-induced deformation of a bound-state energy.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of surviving population in the metastable well
surviving population in the metastable well
tunneling leakage (decay) rate of the metastable state
derivation_notes: Irreversible tunneling escape from a quasi-bound state gives a constant per-particle leakage rate, so the survival probability obeys first-order exponential decay dN/dt = -gamma*N.

states.description: surviving population in the metastable well

scenario_text: An unstable quasi-bound state trapped behind a partial barrier leaks out by tunneling over time. The population remaining in the metastable well is monitored as it depletes. The measurement follows the decay of the survival probability set by the leakage rate. This probes irreversible escape of a metastable quantum state.

symbol_descriptions: time derivative of the in-plane x velocity component
cyclotron angular frequency set by the charge-to-mass ratio and field strength
derivation_notes: The magnetic force F = q v x B rotates the velocity vector at the cyclotron frequency omega = qB/m, giving dvx/dt = omega*vy and dvy/dt = -omega*vx, which conserves speed and yields circular motion.

states.description: x component of particle velocity
y component of particle velocity

scenario_text: A charged particle enters a region of uniform magnetic field oriented perpendicular to its initial velocity. The magnetic force continuously turns the velocity vector without changing its speed, producing circular motion in the plane. We track the two in-plane velocity components as they evolve over time. The strength of the field and the charge-to-mass ratio set the turning rate.

symbol_descriptions: time derivative of the voltage across the discharging capacitor
derivation_notes: For an RC discharge, current I = V/R drains the capacitor charge Q = C*V, giving C dV/dt = -V/R, i.e. dV/dt = -V/(R*C) with relaxation time RC.

states.description: voltage across the capacitor

scenario_text: A capacitor charged to an initial voltage is connected across a resistor, allowing stored charge to drain through the circuit. The rate at which charge leaves the capacitor is proportional to the instantaneous voltage across it. We follow the voltage on the capacitor as it relaxes toward zero. The resistance and capacitance jointly set the relaxation timescale.

symbol_descriptions: electrostatic potential at a given radial distance from the point charge
derivation_notes: Coulomb's law for the electrostatic potential of a point charge, obtained by integrating the radial electric field E = q/(4*pi*epsilon0*r^2) from infinity to r, giving the standard 1/r potential.
scenario_text: A point charge sits at the origin, and we probe the electrostatic potential it produces at various radial distances. The potential is measured along a line moving outward from the charge. The magnitude of the source charge and the surrounding medium set the overall scale. We record how the potential varies with distance as an instantaneous field property.

symbol_descriptions: time derivative of the charge on the capacitor
derivation_notes: Kirchhoff's voltage law for a source-free series RLC loop gives L*dI/dt + R*I + Q/C = 0, with dQ/dt = I coupling charge and current into a closed first-order system.

states.description: charge on the capacitor
current flowing in the loop

scenario_text: A series circuit contains an inductor, a resistor, and a capacitor with no external driving source after an initial disturbance. The charge on the capacitor exchanges energy with the inductor while the resistor dissipates it. We track the capacitor charge and the loop current as they evolve. Component values determine both the natural frequency and the damping.

symbol_descriptions: time derivative of the rod's velocity
velocity of the conducting rod along the rails
derivation_notes: The motional EMF B*L*v drives a current I = B*L*v/R through the loop; this current in the field produces a retarding force F = -B*L*I = -(B^2 L^2 / R) v, giving m dv/dt = -(B^2 L^2 / R) v.

states.description: velocity of the conducting rod along the rails

scenario_text: A conducting rod slides along parallel rails immersed in a fixed magnetic field, and the changing enclosed area drives a current through a resistive loop. The induced current produces a retarding force on the moving rod that opposes its motion. We follow the rod's velocity as it slows. The field strength, rod length, mass, and loop resistance set the braking behavior.

symbol_descriptions: transmitted wave intensity after passing through the absorbing slab
derivation_notes: Beer-Lambert law: dI/dx = -alpha*I, where each layer removes a fraction proportional to local intensity, integrated over thickness x yields exponential attenuation.
scenario_text: A monochromatic electromagnetic wave passes through a slab of absorbing material, and its intensity diminishes with penetration depth. Each layer removes a fraction of the transmitted power proportional to the local intensity. We measure the transmitted intensity as a function of the slab thickness. The absorption coefficient of the medium sets the attenuation scale.

symbol_descriptions: instantaneous electromagnetic power radiated by the accelerating charge
derivation_notes: This is the Larmor formula for the power radiated by a nonrelativistic accelerating point charge, expressed in SI units as P = mu0 q^2 a^2 / (6 pi c).
scenario_text: An accelerating charged particle radiates electromagnetic power that grows with the square of its acceleration. We examine the instantaneous radiated power for particles undergoing different accelerations. The particle charge sets an overall prefactor. Each measurement is an independent snapshot of emission at a given acceleration.

symbol_descriptions: induced electromotive force around the coaxial loop
rate of change of solenoid current
number of turns per unit length
derivation_notes: From Faraday's law emf = -dPhi/dt with B = mu0*n*I inside a long solenoid, so Phi = mu0*n*A*I and the induced emf magnitude is mu0*n*A*dI/dt (sign indicating opposition per Lenz's law).
scenario_text: A long solenoid carries a steadily increasing current, and the changing magnetic flux inside induces an electric field that opposes the flux growth. We record the magnitude of the induced electromotive force around a coaxial loop for different rates of current change. The number of turns and coil geometry set the coupling. Each configuration yields an instantaneous induced voltage.

symbol_descriptions: equilibrium magnetization of the ferromagnetic sample
characteristic field scale of the material
derivation_notes: Mean-field/Langevin-type saturation response where the unaligned domain fraction shrinks with field; the tanh form arises from a two-state alignment model saturating at Msat with characteristic field H0, and dM/dH diminishes as M approaches Msat.
scenario_text: A ferromagnetic sample is placed in an external magnetic field that is slowly increased, and its magnetization rises toward a saturation limit. As more magnetic domains align, the remaining unaligned fraction shrinks and further gains diminish. We measure the equilibrium magnetization at various applied field strengths. The saturation magnetization and a characteristic field set the response curve.

symbol_descriptions: time derivative of the charged particle's drift velocity
drift velocity of the charged particle
derivation_notes: Newton's second law with a constant electric driving force qE and linear viscous drag -b*v; the velocity relaxes exponentially to the terminal drift qE/b.

states.description: drift velocity of the charged particle

scenario_text: A charged particle moves through a viscous medium while being pushed by a constant uniform electric field, reaching a balance between electric force and drag. We track the particle velocity as it accelerates from rest toward its terminal drift value. The field strength, charge, and drag coefficient set the approach. The velocity relaxes smoothly to a steady drift.

symbol_descriptions: Maximum tangential force sustained before sliding onset
Normal load pressing block onto surface
Contact friction coefficient of the surface pairing
derivation_notes: Coulomb's law of static friction: the maximum static friction force is proportional to the normal load, with the static friction coefficient as the proportionality constant.
scenario_text: A block rests on a horizontal surface, and a slowly increasing horizontal pull is applied until the block begins to slide. Experimenters vary the normal load pressing the block down and the surface preparation. They record the maximum tangential force that the contact can sustain just before motion begins. The measured threshold force scales with the pressing load and the contact condition.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the mass velocity along the vertical direction
derivation_notes: Newton's second law for a damped harmonic oscillator: the mass experiences a linear restoring spring force (-k*x) and a viscous drag force proportional to and opposing velocity (-c*v), measured about the gravitational equilibrium position.

states.description: Vertical displacement from equilibrium
Vertical velocity of the mass

scenario_text: A small mass hangs from a spring and oscillates vertically while moving through a viscous surrounding medium that resists its motion. The medium provides a retarding force proportional to speed, gradually removing energy from the motion. Starting from an initial displacement and velocity, the position evolves over time. The behavior depends on the spring stiffness, the mass, and the damping strength.

symbol_descriptions: Horizontal range from launch point to landing at same height
Launch angle above horizontal in radians
derivation_notes: Derived from projectile kinematics under constant gravity: time of flight t = 2*v0*sin(theta)/g times horizontal velocity v0*cos(theta), using sin(2*theta)=2*sin(theta)*cos(theta).
scenario_text: A projectile is launched into air at various speeds and elevation angles from ground level. Neglecting drag, its flight follows a smooth arc under constant downward acceleration. The experimenters record the horizontal distance covered before the projectile returns to launch height. This landing distance depends on launch speed and angle.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of angular velocity of the rotating disk
Angular velocity of the disk about its axle
Tangential force applied at the rim by the cord
Rotational moment of inertia of the disk about its axle
derivation_notes: The wrapped cord applies torque tau = F_applied * R at the rim; Newton's rotational law tau = I_disk * domega_dt gives the constant angular acceleration that builds up omega from rest.

states.description: Angular velocity of the disk about its axle

scenario_text: A uniform disk is free to rotate about a fixed central axle, and a steady tangential force is applied at its rim by a wrapped cord. The applied torque produces an angular acceleration resisted by the disk's rotational inertia. Starting from rest, the angular velocity builds up over time as the cord pulls. The evolution depends on the applied torque and the disk's inertia.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the pendulum angular velocity
Angular displacement from the downward vertical
derivation_notes: The gravitational torque about the pivot yields the nonlinear pendulum equation phi'' = -(g/L) sin(phi); rewriting as a first-order system with omega = phi' gives the closed form.

states.description: Angular displacement from the downward vertical
Angular velocity of the pendulum

scenario_text: A pendulum consisting of a mass on a light rod swings with large amplitude about its pivot under gravity, without small-angle simplification. The restoring effect comes from the gravitational component along the arc, which varies nonlinearly with angle. Starting from a released angle, the system swings back and forth. The motion depends on the rod length and gravity.

symbol_descriptions: Acceleration of the cart along the inclined surface
Incline angle above horizontal in radians
derivation_notes: From Newton's second law on a frictionless incline, the net force along the track is the component of gravity mg*sin(theta), giving a = g*sin(theta).
scenario_text: A cart is released on a frictionless inclined track and slides downward under gravity while carrying a small onboard measurement unit. The component of gravity along the incline sets a constant acceleration determined by the slope angle. Experimenters vary the incline angle and the local gravity and record the along-track acceleration. The response reflects only the geometric projection of gravity.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the orbiting body's velocity component along x
Position coordinate along x relative to central body
Position coordinate along y relative to central body
derivation_notes: Newtonian inverse-square gravity: acceleration points toward the central body with magnitude G*M/r^2, giving components -G*M*x/r^3 and -G*M*y/r^3 where r=sqrt(x^2+y^2).

states.description: Position coordinate along x relative to central body
Position coordinate along y relative to central body
Velocity component along x
Velocity component along y

scenario_text: A small body moves in a bound orbit around a much heavier central body under mutual gravitational attraction, tracked in a plane. The inward pull depends on the inverse square of separation and continuously bends the trajectory. Given an initial position and velocity, the body traces its orbital path over time. The dynamics depend on the central mass and the gravitational constant.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the sphere's downward speed
Downward speed of the falling sphere
derivation_notes: Newton's second law for a falling sphere with quadratic fluid resistance: net downward acceleration equals gravity minus drag force per unit mass, driving the speed toward a terminal velocity where forces balance.

states.description: Downward speed of the falling sphere

scenario_text: A dense sphere falls through a thick fluid column and quickly reaches a steady descent speed where resistance balances gravity. The retarding force grows with speed until motion stabilizes. Starting from rest, the downward speed rises and levels off. The approach depends on the sphere's weight and the fluid's drag characteristics.

symbol_descriptions: Inward radial force needed to maintain circular motion
Angular spin rate of the platform
derivation_notes: Derived from Newton's second law for uniform circular motion: the centripetal acceleration is a = r*omega^2, so the required inward force is F = m*a = m*r*omega^2.
scenario_text: A rotating platform holds a small object that spins with it, and the object is held on a circular path by an inward radial force from a tether. As the spin rate changes, the required inward force to maintain the circular path changes. Experimenters vary the object mass, the radius of the path, and the spin rate, recording the tether tension. The tension reflects the inward force needed for circular motion.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the mass velocity along the track
derivation_notes: Newton's second law with a Duffing-type restoring force F = -k_linear*x - k_cubic*x^3 on a frictionless surface gives m*dv/dt = F and dx/dt = v.

states.description: Displacement from equilibrium
Velocity of the mass

scenario_text: A mass slides on a frictionless surface attached to a spring whose restoring stiffness increases beyond the simple linear regime at large stretch, adding a cubic hardening term. Released from a displacement, the mass oscillates but with a shape and period that shift with amplitude. Starting from initial displacement and velocity, the position evolves over time. The motion depends on the linear stiffness, the hardening coefficient, and the mass.

symbol_descriptions: electrical resistivity of the metal at fixed temperature
concentration of static impurity scattering centers
residual resistivity coefficient per unit impurity concentration
derivation_notes: Matthiessen's rule combines temperature-independent impurity scattering (rho0*n_imp) with the Bloch-Gruneisen phonon term proportional to (T/D)^5 times the integral of x^5/((e^x-1)(1-e^-x)) from 0 to D/T; the low-T limit of that integral gives rho ~ T^5.
scenario_text: A metallic sample is cooled below its transition temperature and its electrical resistance drops as scattering channels freeze out. Experimenters measure the residual electrical resistivity at various temperatures in the low-temperature regime where lattice vibration contributions dominate. Each measurement is an independent equilibrium reading of resistivity at a fixed bath temperature. The goal is to relate the measured resistivity to temperature and the density of scattering centers.

derivation_notes: Derived from the two-level (spin-1/2) paramagnet in the canonical ensemble: minimizing free energy yields the Brillouin/Langevin function, which for J=1/2 reduces to M = N*mu*tanh(mu*B/(kB*T)), naturally saturating at N*mu for strong fields.
scenario_text: In a paramagnetic insulator, the magnetization responds to an applied external magnetic field at fixed temperature. Independent samples are prepared and the equilibrium magnetization is recorded for various field strengths and temperatures. At strong fields the alignment of magnetic moments approaches complete saturation. The task is to model the equilibrium magnetization as a function of field and temperature.

symbol_descriptions: molar specific heat of the crystal
classical Dulong-Petit limit 3*N_A*k_B (molar gas constant scale)
derivation_notes: Einstein model of a dielectric solid: quantized harmonic oscillators of energy k_B*Td give mean energy per mode via Bose-Einstein statistics; differentiating the total vibrational energy with respect to T yields this specific heat, which vanishes as T->0 and approaches the Dulong-Petit limit at high T.
scenario_text: A dielectric crystal is probed by measuring its heat capacity as the temperature is varied across a wide range. At low temperatures the vibrational modes are progressively frozen out, while at high temperatures the heat capacity approaches a classical limit. Each data point is an independent equilibrium measurement at a set temperature. The objective is to express the specific heat in terms of temperature and the vibrational energy scale.

derivation_notes: Arrhenius/Boltzmann thermal activation: the fraction of carriers excited across the energy barrier follows the Boltzmann factor exp(-Ea/kB*T), scaled by the donor prefactor n0.
scenario_text: In a doped semiconductor, mobile charge carriers are thermally excited across an energy barrier that separates bound and free states. Independent samples held at fixed temperatures are measured for their free carrier concentration. As temperature increases, more carriers are activated. The task is to model the carrier density from temperature and the activation energy.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of the temperature excess of the block
temperature excess of the block above the reservoir
thermal relaxation time constant (heat capacity divided by conductance)
derivation_notes: Newtonian cooling: heat flux out is proportional to the temperature excess (conductance * Theta), and the stored energy is C*Theta, giving C*dTheta/dt = -G*Theta, i.e. dTheta/dt = -Theta/tau with tau = C/G.

states.description: temperature excess of the block above the reservoir

scenario_text: A metallic block is suddenly brought into contact with a cold reservoir and its internal temperature relaxes toward equilibrium as heat conducts away. The evolving temperature difference and stored thermal energy jointly change over time as heat flows out. The relaxation is governed by the coupling between the block and its surroundings. The task is to evolve the temperature excess over time from an initial heated state.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of the charge density wave order parameter amplitude
amplitude of the charge density wave order parameter
linear growth rate reflecting proximity below the transition
nonlinear self-limiting coefficient setting the saturation amplitude
derivation_notes: This is the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equation for a real order parameter amplitude: a linear instability drives exponential growth from a small seed while a cubic term self-limits the amplitude, yielding saturation at Psi = sqrt(growth_rate/saturation_coeff).

states.description: amplitude of the charge density wave order parameter

scenario_text: A charge density wave forms in a low-dimensional conductor as its order parameter grows from a small fluctuation and saturates at an equilibrium amplitude below the transition. The amplitude evolves in time driven by a competition between a growth tendency and a self-limiting nonlinear term. Starting from a tiny seed, the pattern strengthens and levels off. The goal is to evolve the order parameter amplitude over time.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of the tracer drift velocity
drift velocity of the suspended tracer
applied driving force on the tracer
effective inertial mass of the tracer
derivation_notes: Newton's second law for a tracer in a viscous metal: inertia balances a constant driving force against linear Stokes-type drag proportional to velocity, yielding relaxation toward a terminal drift F_drive/drag_coeff.

states.description: drift velocity of the suspended tracer

scenario_text: In a viscous liquid metal, a suspended tracer moves under an applied driving force while experiencing frictional drag from the surrounding fluid. Its velocity evolves in time as inertia competes with the velocity-dependent drag. Starting from rest, the tracer accelerates and approaches a terminal drift. The objective is to evolve the tracer velocity over time.

symbol_descriptions: rate of change of the crystal polarization
derivation_notes: A Landau-type ferroelectric with linear restoring and cubic anharmonic self-limiting force undergoing damped oscillation: P'' = -omega0_sq*P - beta*P^3 - gamma*P', recast as first-order in P and u.

states.description: polarization of the ferroelectric crystal
time rate of the polarization

scenario_text: A ferroelectric crystal near its transition has a polarization that responds to an internal restoring tendency and a self-limiting anharmonic term, and the coupled polarization and its rate together determine an underdamped relaxation toward equilibrium. After a small perturbation the polarization oscillates while losing energy to lattice damping. The evolution proceeds from an initial displaced state. The goal is to evolve the polarization over time.

symbol_descriptions: Equilibrium pressure of the interacting gas
Second virial coefficient capturing pairwise interactions
derivation_notes: This is the virial expansion of the equation of state, expressing pressure as an ideal-gas term (k_B*T*rho) plus density corrections from pairwise (B2) and higher-order (B3) interactions.
scenario_text: A gas of weakly interacting particles is confined in a container held at fixed temperature. As the number density of particles is varied while temperature is kept constant, the pressure deviates from the simple proportional relationship expected for an ideal gas. Experimenters measure the equilibrium pressure across a range of densities and temperatures to characterize the correction from pairwise interactions.

symbol_descriptions: Magnetic moment of a single microscopic dipole
derivation_notes: Derived from the statistical mechanics of a spin-1/2 (two-level) paramagnet in a Boltzmann distribution; the mean magnetization follows the Brillouin/Langevin form which for two-state moments reduces to tanh(mu*B/(k_B*T)), giving linear response at small B and saturation at large B.
scenario_text: A paramagnetic solid is placed in an external magnetic field at fixed temperature, and its net magnetization is measured. At weak fields the magnetization grows nearly linearly with field strength, but at strong fields it levels off as the microscopic moments become fully aligned. The experiment records magnetization as the field and temperature are independently tuned.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the sphere's surface temperature
derivation_notes: Energy balance under Stefan-Boltzmann radiative exchange in vacuum: the heat capacity times dT/dt equals the net radiated power proportional to (T^4 - T_wall^4), giving a lumped fourth-power cooling law.

states.description: Surface temperature of the sphere

scenario_text: A hot metal sphere is suspended in a large evacuated enclosure whose walls are held at a low fixed temperature, so heat leaves only by radiative exchange. The sphere's temperature falls over time as it emits thermal radiation, with the loss rate depending strongly on its current temperature. Observers track the surface temperature as it relaxes toward the enclosure temperature.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the first body's temperature
Heat capacity of the first body
Heat capacity of the second body
derivation_notes: Newton's law of cooling for two isolated bodies: heat flows at rate k_cond*(T2-T1), raising T1 at that rate divided by its heat capacity C1 and lowering T2 by the same energy flux divided by C2.

states.description: Temperature of the first body
Temperature of the second body

scenario_text: Two bodies with different heat capacities are brought into thermal contact through a conducting bridge and isolated from the surroundings. Heat flows between them at a rate proportional to their instantaneous temperature difference, and both temperatures evolve until they meet at a common value. The experiment monitors each body's temperature as the pair equilibrates.

symbol_descriptions: Average thermal energy per oscillator mode
Characteristic excitation spacing of the mode
Reduced Planck constant scaling the excitation spacing to energy
derivation_notes: Planck's mean energy of a quantized harmonic oscillator from the Bose-Einstein occupation of energy levels E_n = n*hbar*w; yields U -> kB*T at high T (equipartition) and exponential freeze-out exp(-hbar*w/kB*T) at low T.
scenario_text: A dilute collection of quantized oscillators shares a fixed amount of thermal energy at a given temperature, and the average energy per oscillator is measured. At high temperature the energy grows linearly with temperature, but at low temperature it becomes exponentially suppressed as excitations freeze out. Measurements span a wide temperature range at fixed excitation spacing.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the central peak concentration
Solute concentration at the column center
derivation_notes: For 1D diffusion from an instantaneous plane source, the central concentration follows C(t) = M/sqrt(4*pi*D*t), so C ~ t^(-1/2); differentiating gives dC/dt = -C/(2t), a self-contained ODE for the peak decay as the Gaussian widens.

states.description: Solute concentration at the column center

scenario_text: A solute is released as a thin sheet at the center of a long quiescent column and spreads through the medium by random molecular motion. The peak concentration at the center falls over time as the distribution widens. Observers record the central concentration as diffusion redistributes the solute along the column.

symbol_descriptions: Spontaneous order parameter of the ordered phase
Saturation amplitude of the order parameter
Critical exponent governing the rise near the transition
derivation_notes: From Landau mean-field theory of continuous phase transitions, minimizing the free energy F = a(T-Tc)m^2 + b*m^4 yields m proportional to (Tc-T)^beta near criticality, with beta=1/2 in mean field; the power-law form captures the steep rise below Tc and saturation far below.
scenario_text: A magnetic material near its ordering transition is studied by measuring its spontaneous order parameter as the temperature is tuned below a critical point. Just below the transition the order parameter rises steeply from zero, while far below it saturates. The measurement captures how the ordered fraction depends on how far the system sits beneath the critical temperature.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the temperature nonuniformity amplitude
Amplitude of the dominant temperature variation along the rod
Decay rate of the dominant thermal mode (thermal diffusivity times squared wavenumber)
derivation_notes: For the heat equation with a single dominant spatial Fourier mode in an insulated rod, the mode amplitude obeys dA/dt = -alpha*k^2*A, giving exponential decay toward the uniform state with lumped rate constant decay_rate.

states.description: Amplitude of the dominant temperature variation along the rod

scenario_text: An initially uneven temperature profile in a thin insulated rod smooths out as heat conducts internally, and a single dominant spatial variation decays away. The amplitude of the temperature nonuniformity is tracked as the rod approaches a uniform state. The decay proceeds without any external heating or cooling.

symbol_descriptions: Equilibrium vapor pressure above the liquid
Characteristic latent energy scale of vaporization
derivation_notes: Integration of the Clausius-Clapeyron relation dP/dT = L*P/(R*T^2) assuming constant latent heat and ideal-gas vapor yields the Arrhenius-type exponential vapor pressure law.
scenario_text: A vessel of liquid is in equilibrium with its vapor, and the vapor pressure above the surface is measured as the temperature is varied. The pressure rises sharply and nonlinearly as temperature increases, reflecting the energy cost of moving molecules into the gas phase. The experiment records vapor pressure over a moderate temperature range at fixed latent energy scale.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the particle count in the first compartment
Number of particles in the first compartment
Effective per-particle hopping rate through the opening
Fixed total number of particles in the container
derivation_notes: Net flux across the opening is proportional to the population imbalance (n leaving minus (N_total - n) arriving), driving n toward the equal split N_total/2 as the maximum-entropy equilibrium.

states.description: Number of particles in the first compartment

scenario_text: A container is divided into two compartments connected by a small opening, holding a fixed total number of gas particles that hop between sides. Starting from an uneven split, the particle count in one compartment relaxes toward an even balance driven by the greater number of accessible microstates near equality. Observers track the population of one compartment as it evolves toward balance.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the number of surviving parent nuclei
Decay constant (transition probability per unit time)
derivation_notes: Radioactive decay through a single channel: the depletion rate is proportional to the current population with a fixed decay constant, yielding exponential decay.

states.description: Number of surviving parent nuclei

scenario_text: A sample of unstable nuclei is prepared and left to decay without replenishment. The number of surviving parent nuclei is monitored over time. The decay proceeds through a single dominant channel with a fixed transition probability per unit time. The observed depletion reflects the intrinsic instability of the nuclear state.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the daughter nuclide population
Decay constant of the parent nuclide
Decay constant of the daughter nuclide
derivation_notes: Standard Bateman two-step decay chain: the parent decays exponentially feeding the daughter, while the daughter simultaneously decays into the stable product.

states.description: Number of parent nuclei
Number of daughter nuclei

scenario_text: In a decay chain, a parent nuclide decays into a radioactive daughter, which itself decays into a stable product. Both the parent and daughter populations evolve simultaneously from initial stocks. The daughter first accumulates as it is fed by the parent, then declines as its own decay dominates. The interplay of two distinct transition rates governs the buildup and decline.

symbol_descriptions: Transmitted beam intensity after traversing the material
derivation_notes: Beer-Lambert attenuation law: dI/dx = -n*sigma*I integrated over thickness gives exponential decay with linear attenuation coefficient mu = n*sigma.
scenario_text: A beam of particles passes through a slab of absorbing material with a fixed number density of scattering centers. The transmitted intensity decreases with the thickness traversed due to a constant interaction cross section. Experimenters vary the slab thickness and the cross section to measure attenuation. The output is the fraction of the beam that survives passage.

symbol_descriptions: Total relativistic energy of the particle
Particle speed as a fraction of the limiting velocity
derivation_notes: From special relativity, total energy E = gamma*m*c^2 with the Lorentz factor gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - (v_actual/c)^2); since v is expressed as a fraction of the limiting velocity, (v_actual/c) = v, giving E = m*c^2/sqrt(1 - v^2), which diverges as v -> 1.
scenario_text: The total energy of a relativistic particle is examined as its speed approaches a fundamental limiting velocity. The particle has a fixed rest mass, and its energy is measured as a function of speed. As the speed grows the energy climbs steeply and diverges near the limit. The relationship reflects the relativistic scaling of inertia.

symbol_descriptions: Scattering cross section near the resonance
derivation_notes: This is the Breit-Wigner (Lorentzian) resonance formula from nuclear/particle scattering theory, giving a symmetric peak of height sigma0 at E=Er with full-width-at-half-maximum equal to Gamma.
scenario_text: A resonance appears in a scattering experiment as the collision energy is scanned across a narrow region. The reaction rate peaks sharply when the energy matches the resonance value and falls off symmetrically on either side. The peak height and width are set by the resonance parameters. The measured cross section traces out the resonant response.

derivation_notes: Semi-empirical mass formula (Bethe-Weizsacker liquid-drop model) divided by A: volume term minus surface, Coulomb, and asymmetry penalties plus a parity-dependent pairing correction.
scenario_text: The binding energy per nucleon is studied as a function of mass number across the chart of nuclides. Competing volume, surface, and charge contributions combine to produce a curve that rises, peaks, and gently declines. The proton number relative to mass number modulates the charge penalty. The output captures how tightly bound nuclei are on average.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of kinetic energy loss along the trajectory
Kinetic energy of the traversing particle
Stopping-power coefficient combining electron density and coupling constants
Reference mean excitation energy of the medium
Dimensionless offset ensuring the logarithm stays positive at low energy
derivation_notes: This is a Bethe-like stopping power model where dE/dx (here parameterized along t as the trajectory coordinate) scales as (1/E)*ln(E/I), so energy loss per unit path rises sharply as the particle slows toward rest.

states.description: Kinetic energy of the traversing particle

scenario_text: A charged particle penetrates a stopping medium and loses kinetic energy through interactions with the medium's electrons. The energy loss per unit path length depends strongly on the particle's instantaneous kinetic energy, rising as the particle slows. The particle's energy is followed as it traverses the material until it nears rest. The stopping behavior governs the depth profile of deposited energy.

symbol_descriptions: Survival probability of the original flavor state
Oscillation phase constant (1.27 in GeV^2/(eV^2 km) natural units)
derivation_notes: Standard two-flavor neutrino oscillation formula derived from coherent quantum superposition of two mass eigenstates; the survival probability is 1 minus the transition probability sin^2(2theta) sin^2(dm2 L / 4E), with k_osc absorbing the unit conversion factor.
scenario_text: A two-state neutral particle system oscillates between two distinct flavor identities as it propagates. The probability of detecting the original flavor varies periodically with the distance traveled and the energy of the beam. The oscillation frequency is set by a small mass-squared difference between the underlying states. The measured survival probability reveals the coherent mixing.

symbol_descriptions: Rate of change of the free neutron population
Free neutron population in the assembly
Effective neutron multiplication factor per generation
Mean neutron generation time between fission generations
derivation_notes: Each generation multiplies the neutron count by k_eff, giving a net change of (k_eff - 1) per generation over the mean generation time; this yields exponential growth, steady state, or decay depending on whether k_eff exceeds, equals, or is below unity.

states.description: Free neutron population in the assembly

scenario_text: Fissile nuclei in a multiplying assembly release neutrons that induce further fissions, while a fraction of neutrons is lost to absorption and leakage. The neutron population evolves according to the net multiplication per generation and the mean time between generations. Depending on the effective multiplication factor, the population can grow, hold steady, or die away. The count of free neutrons is tracked from an initial seed.

symbol_descriptions: Fusion reaction rate per unit volume
Number density of the first reacting species
Number density of the second reacting species
Temperature-dependent reactivity (averaged cross-section times relative velocity)
Kronecker delta factor accounting for identical-species double counting
derivation_notes: Standard fusion reaction rate density R = n1*n2*<sigma*v>/(1+delta12), where the product of reactant number densities times the reactivity gives the volumetric rate; the (1+delta12) factor avoids double-counting for identical species.
scenario_text: In a fusion plasma the reaction rate per unit volume depends on the number densities of the reacting nuclei and a temperature-dependent reactivity. Experimenters vary the fuel densities and the reactivity to predict the volumetric energy yield. The rate rises with the product of the reacting species concentrations. The output quantifies how quickly fusion energy is produced.

symbol_descriptions: Time derivative of the excess carrier density
Excess carrier density relative to equilibrium
Mean collective drift momentum of the carriers
Coupling of drift momentum into density relaxation
Coupling of density imbalance into momentum evolution
derivation_notes: The excess density relaxes exponentially through collisions while receiving a transient contribution from the collective drift momentum; the drift momentum similarly relaxes and is driven by the population imbalance, giving a linearly coupled relaxation pair.

states.description: Excess carrier density relative to equilibrium
Mean collective drift momentum of the carriers

scenario_text: In a conducting solid, an initial nonuniform population of charge carriers is prepared and then allowed to redistribute under internal scattering and drift processes. The carrier density and the associated internal drift momentum relax back toward equilibrium as collisions dissipate the excess and coupling between the population imbalance and the collective momentum produces transient adjustment. We track how the excess carrier density and the mean drift momentum jointly evolve in time after the perturbation is removed. The interest is in the coupled relaxation dynamics governed by scattering within the electronic subsystem.

symbol_descriptions: Heat storage capacity per unit volume in the low-temperature regime
Debye (vibrational cutoff) temperature of the material
Number density of atoms per unit volume
derivation_notes: Debye T^3 law: at T << Theta the low-frequency acoustic phonon modes dominate, and integrating the Debye phonon spectrum gives C_v = (12*pi^4/5) n k_B (T/Theta)^3.
scenario_text: A crystalline insulator is cooled to very low temperatures, and its ability to store thermal energy is measured as the lattice temperature is varied. At low temperatures the collective vibrational modes of the lattice dominate the response, and the amount of stored energy per unit temperature change reflects how these modes become progressively excited. The measured heat storage capacity rises steeply from near zero as temperature increases before the low-temperature regime ends. The goal is to capture how this capacity depends on temperature deep in the cold regime.
